title: 'Not Delhi, not Pindi': Tarique Rahman repeats warning at Army Stadium, leads BNP march
dek: Bangladesh's prime minister told a national day event that no one must again make the country a 'subservient state', then led his party's first big Dhaka march since taking power. The Ganges water treaty expires in five weeks.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Bangladesh's Prime Minister Tarique Rahman told a state ceremony in Dhaka on Saturday that the country's pledge on 7 November must be that no one can again turn Bangladesh into "a subservient state", ending his speech with the line he first used in his holiday message on Friday: "Not Delhi, not Pindi, not anyone else - Bangladesh first." Pindi, short for Rawalpindi, is the seat of Pakistan's army.

He then led his Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) through central Dhaka in its first big street march since taking office in February.

The line comes as India and Bangladesh have five weeks left to agree on the future of the Ganges water-sharing treaty, which expires on 12 December, and with no date yet fixed for Mr Rahman's first visit to India as prime minister. 

## The 7 November messages

Bangladesh marks 7 November as National Revolution and Solidarity Day. It commemorates the 1975 uprising by soldiers that followed a counter-coup on 3 November and brought Ziaur Rahman, the BNP's founder and Mr Rahman's father, to power. Successive governments have marked the day very differently: the BNP celebrates it, while the Awami League, which governed from 2009 until Sheikh Hasina was ousted in August 2024, did not treat it as a holiday.

In his message, Mr Rahman said that in 1975 "the soldiers and people of Bangladesh united to thwart all conspiracies against the country's independence and sovereignty". He said the "defeated forces" of that time, in the name of the "Grand Alliance", had later "turned the country into a subservient state following a prolonged course of conspiracy". The Grand Alliance was the coalition led by the Awami League. The message did not name India, Ms Hasina or the Awami League, but referred to a "fascist regime" and "one-party authoritarian rule". The BNP has long accused the Hasina government of being too close to New Delhi.

President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir, in his own message, said the day "remains an unforgettable day in our national life" and that "our beloved motherland was once again saved from the peril of becoming a subservient state". He also called for mutual respect and dialogue in resolving national problems.

## Saturday's speech

Mr Rahman was chief guest at the government's National Revolution and Solidarity Day event at the Army Stadium in Banani, organised under the Ministry of Defence, with the chiefs of the three armed services and foreign diplomats present, according to the state news agency BSS. About 3,000 cadets of the Bangladesh National Cadet Corps and 500 Scouts took part in a display.

"National unity is needed to keep this pledge," he said. He said the struggles of 1971, 1975, 1990 and the 2024 uprising showed that the people "never compromise on national interest, independence or sovereignty". The war of 1971 "was to win independence, and fight in 2024 was to protect it", he said. He accused forces defeated in 1975 of having later regrouped and again turned the country into a subservient state, and said the honour of the armed forces had been damaged by the killing of army officers in the 2009 Pilkhana mutiny. As in his Friday message, he did not name India, Sheikh Hasina or the Awami League; Delhi was the only reference to India.

## The march

The BNP procession left the party's central office at Naya Paltan at about 3.15 pm Dhaka time (2.45 pm IST) with Mr Rahman, who is also party chairman, at its head, according to reports. The route was changed to end at Zia Udyan, the burial site of Ziaur Rahman, rather than at Manik Mia Avenue as first announced. The party held processions in other districts and cities on the same day, with local marches to follow on Sunday. No crowd estimate had been published, and no incidents had been reported by late afternoon.

## The backdrop

The party's programme runs from 5 to 11 November. Reports describe a tense backdrop: friction with an opposition alliance of 11 parties, flash protests by activists of the banned Awami League, crude bomb explosions during some processions, and continuing unrest among garment workers. Ms Hasina, who has lived in India since August 2024 and has been sentenced to death in absentia by a Dhaka tribunal, has said she will return to Bangladesh in December. A BNP leader in Dhaka was quoted as saying that if she returns, "the people of the entire country will deal with her".

## Why it matters for India and Bengal

The Ganges treaty, signed in December 1996, sets out how the river's dry-season flow at the Farakka barrage in West Bengal's Murshidabad district is shared between the two countries. It expires on 12 December. On 3 November the Ministry of External Affairs said only that the Joint Rivers Commission was the forum for talks on shared rivers; no meeting has been announced. Bangladesh's water resources minister has said Dhaka wants a new or revised treaty with a guaranteed share before the deadline. Any new arrangement affects the water available to Kolkata port and to farms and towns downstream of Farakka.

India has invited Mr Rahman to visit, but no date has been set. Mr Rahman skipped the BRICS summit in New Delhi earlier this year despite an invitation, and Dhaka sent no representative.

## What happens next

New Delhi has not commented on Mr Rahman's remarks. The BNP's week of events ends on 11 November. The Ganges treaty expires on 12 December unless the two governments agree on an extension or a replacement.
